title: Leg 52 — Yellow Pine to Challis Basin
subtitle: Lick Creek, Yellow Pine, central Idaho backcountry, Panther Creek and the Challis Basin
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. Today we're leaving McCall for a high-country crossing into central Idaho. We'll climb past the forested Lick Creek country, turn south through Yellow Pine, then spend a long stretch over some of Idaho's most remote mountain terrain before reaching Panther Creek. From there the country opens toward the Salmon River and the Challis Basin. Along the way we'll have backcountry communities, mining history, wilderness, stream restoration, old volcanic country, and one of Idaho's most memorable earthquakes. I'll stay quiet while you taxi and depart. Once you're airborne and settled, say Trip resume.

waypoints.name: Lick Creek Pass
viewingNotes: Lick Creek Canyon runs through densely wooded mountain slopes.

waypoints.name: Yellow Pine Valley Pass
viewingNotes: Yellow Pine lies in the meadow valley; rugged Frank Church country fills the broader eastern horizon.

waypoints.name: Panther Creek Traverse
viewingNotes: Panther Creek occupies a steep, forested valley in the Salmon River drainage.

waypoints.name: Challis Basin Approach
viewingNotes: The terrain opens into the Upper Salmon River and Challis Basin country.

blocks.title: Leaving McCall and Payette Lake
blocks.spokenLabel: the high country east of McCall
blocks.text: McCall and Payette Lake are falling behind us as we climb into the mountains east of town. The open water and broad valley disappear quickly here; central Idaho rises into a maze of forested ridges, granite peaks and deeply cut drainages. This is the kind of country where a few miles on the map can mean a very long trip on the ground.

blocks.title: Payette National Forest
blocks.text: Most of the country around us belongs to the Payette National Forest, more than two million acres ranging from dry grasslands to peaks near nine thousand five hundred feet. The forest reaches from Hells Canyon into the edge of the Frank Church wilderness, so this single national forest spans an unusually wide range of Idaho terrain.

blocks.title: Granite under the forests
blocks.text: Beneath much of this mountain country is the Idaho batholith, an enormous body of granitic rock that formed deep underground tens of millions of years ago. Uplift and erosion eventually exposed it. From the air, that geologic foundation helps explain the pale rocky ridges, steep creek valleys and scattered alpine basins that keep appearing between the trees.

blocks.title: A landscape built around valleys rather than roads
blocks.text: Roads become sparse very quickly east of McCall. In this part of Idaho, creek valleys are the natural corridors through terrain that otherwise rises sharply in every direction. Lick Creek is one of those corridors, threading through heavily forested mountains toward the higher country ahead.

blocks.title: Lick Creek country
blocks.text: We are coming into the Lick Creek drainage now. Look for the long forested cut running through the mountains rather than one single landmark. The creek itself can be difficult to pick out continuously beneath the trees, but the valley it occupies is much easier to follow from above.

blocks.title: Following Lick Creek
blocks.text: Lick Creek Canyon should be one of the clearer geographic shapes in this section: a narrow green corridor hemmed in by high wooded slopes. The water may vanish under tree cover, but the drainage keeps its form, bending through country that feels increasingly removed from McCall.

blocks.title: Glacial basins in the high country
blocks.text: The higher ridges around this part of central Idaho hold numerous small lakes and cirques left by mountain glaciers. Many are too small to stand out from ten thousand feet, but the bowl-shaped basins and bare rock around them are often visible. They are reminders that ice helped sharpen a landscape later covered again by forest.

blocks.title: Why the forest breaks apart with elevation
blocks.text: Notice how the tree cover thins as the ridges rise. Elevation, wind, snowpack and exposed rock break the forest into patches near the highest ground. Down in the drainages, moisture and shelter allow much denser stands, so the topography is almost traced in green from the air.

blocks.title: Across the Lick Creek high country
blocks.text: The Lick Creek high country is just ahead. Beyond it, the landscape begins to open toward the remote communities and river headwaters around Yellow Pine. The next few minutes trade one forested drainage for another, with very little flat ground between them.

blocks.title: Toward Yellow Pine
blocks.text: South of the pass, we are entering the Yellow Pine backcountry. Settlement here has always been shaped by isolation. Mining camps, ranches and tiny communities survived by following the few valleys that offered room for roads, buildings and winter travel.

blocks.title: A backcountry trading center
blocks.text: Yellow Pine grew in the early twentieth century as a small trading center for miners and prospectors working the surrounding mountains. It served people moving between claims, camps and the Stibnite district farther east. Even today it remains an unincorporated community rather than a conventional incorporated town.

blocks.title: The harmonica town
blocks.text: Yellow Pine has one of Idaho's more improbable traditions: a harmonica festival. It began in 1990 as part of Idaho's centennial celebration and kept going after the original one-time event proved popular. The instrument fits the place unusually well; miners could carry a harmonica in a pocket and bring music into camps far from any town.

blocks.title: Stibnite and wartime minerals
blocks.text: The mountains east of Yellow Pine also contain the historic Stibnite mining district. Gold was important, but antimony and tungsten made the district nationally significant during the world wars. At its wartime peak Stibnite supported a surprisingly complete company town with housing, a school, hospital and recreation facilities deep in the Idaho backcountry.

blocks.title: Yellow Pine below
blocks.text: Yellow Pine should be close now in the meadowed valley below. Compared with the forest around it, the community is tiny: a loose cluster of buildings and roads surrounded almost immediately by mountains. The broader wild country beyond the valley is every bit as important to the view as the village itself.

blocks.title: The edge of the Frank Church wilderness
blocks.text: The immense roadless country around Yellow Pine connects into the Frank Church–River of No Return Wilderness. At roughly two point three million acres, it is the largest contiguous federally managed wilderness in the lower forty-eight states. Its scale is easier to understand from the air, where ridges and canyons continue for mile after mile with almost no sign of settlement.

blocks.title: Why the Salmon became the River of No Return
blocks.text: The wilderness takes part of its name from the Salmon River, historically called the River of No Return. Early river travelers could descend the fast current in wooden boats, but hauling those boats back upstream through the canyon was often impractical. The nickname captures how strongly the rivers dictated movement through central Idaho.

blocks.title: Airplanes changed Idaho backcountry life
blocks.text: Central Idaho also developed a distinctive aviation culture. Remote ranches, lodges and communities came to rely on small backcountry airstrips because flying could turn days of difficult ground travel into a short hop. From this altitude those strips can be nearly invisible, but aviation remains part of how people live and work in this country.

blocks.title: Gold rush country beyond the ridges
blocks.text: These mountains were repeatedly pulled into mining booms. Around the turn of the twentieth century, the Thunder Mountain gold rush drew thousands of hopeful miners into extremely remote country east of Yellow Pine. Towns appeared quickly, fortunes proved much harder to find, and many of the camps faded almost as fast as they had grown.

blocks.title: Fire as part of the mountain landscape
blocks.text: Long stretches of forest here can look uniform from high altitude, but fire has been constantly rewriting the pattern. Old burns open patches of grass and young trees, while mature stands survive in other drainages. Over decades those patches create a mosaic that can be easier to see from the cockpit than from the ground.

blocks.title: Toward Panther Creek
blocks.text: The terrain ahead begins feeding into the Panther Creek drainage, one of the tributary systems of the Salmon River. The valleys remain steep and narrow, but the drainage network becomes a useful guide through the mountains. Panther Creek itself has an unusually dramatic environmental history tied to mining farther upstream.

blocks.title: The Blackbird Mine legacy
blocks.text: The Blackbird Mine in this drainage produced copper and cobalt over many decades. Waste and acidic runoff carried metals into tributaries and eventually Panther Creek. By the later twentieth century, long stretches of the stream had lost fish and much of their aquatic insect life.

blocks.title: A stream that came back
blocks.text: Panther Creek later became a remarkable restoration story. Cleanup work beginning in the nineteen-nineties sharply reduced metal contamination, and fish returned. U.S. Geological Survey studies found that salmonid populations recovered within roughly a dozen years, including Chinook salmon, steelhead, rainbow trout and bull trout.

blocks.title: Panther Creek valley
blocks.text: Panther Creek is close now. Look for the steep valley itself rather than expecting an uninterrupted view of the water; trees and canyon walls can hide the stream repeatedly. The drainage is the larger feature, cutting a long green seam through otherwise rugged mountain slopes.

blocks.title: From Panther Creek toward open basin country
blocks.text: Beyond Panther Creek, the character of central Idaho starts changing again. Dense forest gives way in places to drier slopes, exposed rock and broader valleys. We are moving toward the Upper Salmon country, where the landscape around Challis is noticeably more open than the high forests behind us.

blocks.title: Central Idaho once had major volcanic fields
blocks.text: Some of the colorful and broken terrain ahead belongs to the Challis volcanic story. About fifty-two to forty-five million years ago, central Idaho experienced widespread volcanism unrelated to the much younger Yellowstone hotspot. Lava flows, ash eruptions and intrusive magma affected an area of roughly ten thousand square miles.

blocks.title: Volcanoes and mineral wealth
blocks.text: That ancient magmatism also helped concentrate mineral deposits. Gold, silver and molybdenum occur in places associated with the Challis volcanic system and its faults. The mining history around Challis is therefore tied not just to human luck and persistence, but to a much older geologic process beneath the mountains.

blocks.title: The Upper Salmon River country
blocks.text: The Salmon River becomes the dominant geographic feature as the basin opens. Around Challis it is no longer buried in the enormous wilderness canyon farther downstream. Instead, the river winds through a broader valley with cottonwoods, ranch land and dry volcanic hills rising around it.

blocks.title: The Challis Basin opens ahead
blocks.text: The Challis Basin should be opening ahead now. After so much enclosed mountain terrain, the wider floor is unmistakable. The town, river, irrigated ground and pale dry slopes sit together in one broad scene, with higher ranges enclosing the basin at a distance.

blocks.title: Challis grew as a supply center
blocks.text: Challis grew in the eighteen-seventies after gold discoveries brought miners into the surrounding mountains. Its location in the basin made it a logical supply center for mining camps as well as ranches and farms. It eventually became the seat of Custer County and remains the commercial center for a huge, sparsely populated part of central Idaho.

blocks.title: Human history far older than the mining boom
blocks.text: The human story here reaches much farther back than mining. Near Challis, archaeological work at the bison kill site uncovered the bones of about thirty bison along with stone tools and points from different periods. The site is a reminder that people were using this valley for hunting and travel long before modern settlement.

blocks.title: The 1983 Borah Peak earthquake
blocks.text: Challis also sits in the memory of Idaho's most damaging recorded earthquake. On October twenty-eighth, 1983, the Borah Peak earthquake violently shook this region. Rockfalls and large boulders struck Challis, and two children were killed when masonry collapsed. The quake permanently shifted parts of the Lost River fault landscape southeast of here.

blocks.title: Challis Airport
blocks.text: Challis Airport is coming up in the open basin just northeast of town, at a little over five thousand feet elevation. After the forests and narrow mountain drainages behind us, the broad valley makes the final arrival feel almost spacious. I'll leave you to the landing from here. When you're finished at Challis, say Trip destination.
